Miguel Hidalgo. The Mexican Catholic priest whose 1810 Grito de Dolores—the Cry of Dolores—launched the Mexican War of Independence against Spanish colonial rule. Though executed before independence was won, he became the symbolic father of Mexican nationhood.

On September 16, 1810, Hidalgo rang the church bell in Dolores and issued his cry for rebellion against Spanish rule. He mobilised tens of thousands of indigenous and mestizo peasants in the Bajío region, creating a mass independence movement unlike any Spain had faced in the colony. In territories under his control, he abolished slavery and forced labour, positioning independence not merely as political separation but as a social revolution. He was captured by Spanish forces, tried for heresy, and executed by firing squad in Chihuahua in July 1811, becoming a martyr to the cause. Every year on September 16, Mexico celebrates Día de la Independencia, marking the day of his uprising. Though Hidalgo did not live to see independence, which was won in 1821, his rebellion fundamentally transformed Mexican society and consciousness. Agustín de Iturbide would complete the work Hidalgo began, and Benito Juárez would later embody the democratic ideals of the nation that Hidalgo had helped to imagine.
